recommendation: Build an original offline technical-quiz package centered on literal answer labels, per-choice feedback and an attempt receipt tied to the quiz content digest. A local verification command should regrade the supplied answers against the matching quiz and reject accidental version mismatches.
selectionCaveat: Generic standalone quizzes, answer explanations, retries and result exports already exist. The selected convenience is the combination of strict content identity and independently recomputed receipts in a small developer package. No uniqueness or star outcome is claimed.

candidates.name: QuizReceipt

evidence.summary: A technical-lesson user says quiz options paraphrased code identifiers and grading returned only an aggregate score. They request literal answer choices and accessible per-question correct/incorrect/unanswered feedback and explanations.
The reporter adds a PowerShell variable-scope example and says the lesson was locally corrected. This validates the usability problem rather than establishing demand for a new standalone package.

candidates.distinctValue: Require exact option text, preserve stable option identifiers, produce an offline quiz, and export a digest-bound attempt that can be regraded locally. Reviewed alternatives already cover much of the quiz player experience. Their reviewed READMEs do not describe the proposed content-bound verification command; this is a scoped comparison, not proof of absence.
candidates.demo: A labeled synthetic technical quiz opens as one HTML file. Wrong, correct and unanswered states plus explanations can be tried immediately; the same receipt can be regraded using the CLI.
candidates.discoverability: Technical educators and developers generating lessons with agents are an identifiable audience in the skill tracker. Concrete screenshots and a downloadable quiz make the result understandable. This is an editorial audience-fit judgment.
candidates.risks: Quiz authors remain responsible for answer correctness. Content digests detect version mismatches; editable receipts and embedded answer keys provide no identity, proctoring or exam-integrity proof.

candidates.name: Shell argument diagnostic worksheet

evidence.summary: A Windows Python launch report shows a path with spaces arriving with literal quote characters.
A macOS report describes the same extra-quote launch problem. Both issues were closed and routed to the Python extension; closure does not establish a fix.

candidates.distinctValue: Could compare intended argv against observed argument capture and explain extra quote characters. Existing process inspectors and shell-argument visualizers cover substantial parts of this task.
candidates.demo: A static synthetic argument comparison is immediate; faithful cross-shell execution and real captures add installation and platform work.
candidates.discoverability: Searches around spaces in filenames and literal quoting failures are concrete, but generic argv visualization has direct competitors.
candidates.risks: A simplified parser can misrepresent PowerShell/native-process and Windows command-line rules. Actual runtime capture improves evidence while reducing the instant-demo advantage.

candidates.name: PromQL matcher-change preview

evidence.summary: A user reports label-matcher set/delete commands mishandling metric names, regex name matchers and consecutive matchers.

candidates.distinctValue: A focused before/after matcher-intent view could make rewrite surprises visible. Prometheus already has query explanation functionality, and safe rewriting requires an up-to-date parser.
candidates.demo: Synthetic queries can show selector changes offline. Correct parsing and faithful display across PromQL syntax substantially expand the complete first-version scope.
candidates.discoverability: Monitoring engineers have strong query-specific search intent, but the audience is narrower and existing Prometheus tooling is established.
candidates.risks: A partial parser can silently misread valid expressions. Version compatibility matters and the live-server behavior would still need separate tests.
